outcomes.text: I found him retired and unrepentant. I said what I had come to say and left him with it.
I found him, and he had spent those years trying to reopen it himself. I did not know where to put that.

title: The other half
text: Your birth parent invites you to meet the rest of their family.

outcomes.text: I met half-siblings who look like me. I have two families now.
I went, and they were strangers with my nose. Everyone was kind and nobody knew what to say.
I said not yet. They said they'd wait.
I said not yet, and by the time I was ready the person who had invited me had died.

choices.label: Go, but take your own family with you

outcomes.text: I brought everybody. Two families met in one kitchen and it was loud and fine.
Bringing them made it a performance. Everyone was polite and nobody said anything true.

title: Everybody's cousin
text: Since the jackpot, relatives you haven't seen in years keep asking for "loans".

outcomes.text: I gave away $2 million. Most of it was never mentioned again.
I gave to everyone who asked, and the asking did not stop. It stopped when the money did.
I said no. Family gatherings got very quiet.
I said no to all of it, and the two people who never asked are the two I still speak to.
I set up trusts for the people I love and a firm no for everyone else.
The advisor handled the family beautifully and put a worrying amount of the rest into something I did not understand.

title: The results
text: The doctor has your latest scan results.

outcomes.text: Remission. I cried in the parking lot for an hour.
It's spread. The doctor says to get my affairs in order.

choices.label: Have the doctor read them to you

outcomes.text: She read it out and then said the word 'remission' twice because I did not react the first time.
She read it out carefully, and then explained what the next round would involve.

choices.label: Leave the envelope shut for a week

outcomes.text: I had one ordinary week first. Whatever the paper said, I got to keep that week.
I waited a week, and the week cost me the start of the treatment they had been hoping to begin at once.

title: Vindicated
text: The company was convicted. Whistleblower law entitles you to a share of the fine.

outcomes.text: I received $2.4 million and a lot of handshakes.
The award was $2.4 million and the legal fees, the tax and the four years took most of the shine off it.

choices.label: Give it to the people downstream

outcomes.text: I put all of it into the towns along that river. My name is on a water treatment plant.
I gave it away and the fund was run badly by people I had trusted to do it properly.

choices.label: Take it and go somewhere nobody knows

outcomes.text: I took the money and moved somewhere with no reason to have heard of me. It was the quietest twenty years of my life.
I took it and left, and found out that the thing I had wanted to get away from travelled with me.

title: Implicated
text: The poisoning scandal broke. Your emails prove you knew.

outcomes.text: I testified and kept my freedom, if not my reputation.
I cooperated fully and the prosecutors decided my emails made me a defendant rather than a witness.
They had the emails.
I denied it, and the emails turned out to have been sent from an account four people shared. It was not enough to charge me.
I resigned on the Friday and the story broke on the Monday without my name in the first paragraph.
Resigning that week looked exactly like what it was, and the prosecutors said so in open court.

title: The rightful heirs
text: A family claims the treasure you found was their grandfather's and is suing you.

outcomes.text: I gave them half.
I settled quickly and cheaply, and then another branch of the family read about the settlement.
I won. Finders keepers, the judge said, more or less.
I lost and paid it all back, plus costs.
I handed the lot over. Their grandfather's name is on a museum case because of it.
I gave it all back and their lawyer still billed me for the fortnight it took to arrange.

title: A letter from prison
text: Your old accountant writes from prison. He says he knows where the rest of the money is.

outcomes.text: He told me. I recovered $200,000.
It was a con to get me to put money on his books.
I threw it out.
I threw it out, and he wrote again every year until the letters stopped coming, which told me the rest.

choices.label: Send the letter to the police

outcomes.text: The fraud squad read it with great interest. Some of the money came home.
He had written it knowing I would pass it on. It named two of my own directors, accurately.

title: Half-siblings
text: Your ex's secret children found you. They want to know their half-siblings.

outcomes.text: The kids got along instantly. Kids are better at this than adults.
I let them meet, and my own children wanted to know why I had never told them. That was the harder conversation.
I said no. It's still too raw.
I said no, and my children found them on their own six years later and said nothing to me about it for a while.
I met them alone in a café and found out they were as confused as I was. It made the rest easier.
I met them first and they wanted things from me I was never going to be able to give.

title: They found the car
text: Detectives traced the paint on the victim's clothes to your car.

outcomes.text: I confessed. It was almost a relief.
I confessed, and the family asked the court for leniency. I did not know what to do with that.
They had the paint, the camera and my phone records.
I denied it, and the paint match was thrown out over how the sample had been stored. I walked out of that courtroom and have never slept properly since.

choices.label: Go to them before the police do

outcomes.text: I went to the family first and said it to their faces. The court heard about that, and so did I, for the rest of my life.
I went to their door and they called the police from the hallway while I was still talking.
